title: Physics-Based AI Video Detection
tagline: Detects AI video via Snell's law + Moiré geometry — no classifier, no training data
description: A proof-of-concept forensics system that detects AI-generated video using physical laws rather than learned classifiers. Two passive props placed in the scene — a drinking glass and a printed fringe board — each impose a hard geometric constraint that real video must satisfy and AI video consistently fails.
longDescription: Tested against Kling AI on the same scene: Snell refraction score 0.862 (authentic threshold ≥0.88), Moiré phase std 0.360 rad (authentic threshold ≤0.04 rad), yielding an overall AI GENERATED verdict. 36% of frames flagged AI GENERATED, 57% UNCERTAIN, 7% AUTHENTIC. Research in progress — aiming for CVPR 2027.
highlights: No training data, no classifier, no learning — detection is purely geometric constraint checking
Auto-mode switching: reads gyroscope in real time, uses Totem (still camera) or Moiré (moving camera) automatically
Totem: Snell's law (n=1.5 glass, n=1.0 air) predicts exact refraction geometry — AI video scores drop and become erratic across frames
Moiré board: ArUco marker tracking constrains fringe phase shift to camera displacement — AI video hallucinates phase variance uncorrelated with motion
Sliding-window Pearson correlation classifies per-window as REAL / UNCERTAIN / AI GENERATED with confidence score
Extensible — same principle applies to shadow geometry, specular reflection, fluid dynamics, any scene element with known physics
inspiration: Every existing AI video detector I could find is a classifier trained on a dataset of real vs AI videos. That approach has a fundamental problem: it chases the output of current models and goes stale as generators improve. I wanted something based on a constraint that can't be learned away — physics. A glass refracts light by Snell's law regardless of how good the generator gets. That law doesn't change with a model update.
challenges: The hardest part was making the Moiré phase measurement robust to real-world noise. Camera shake, slight prop movement, and compression artifacts all add phase variance that looks like a detection signal. The solution was incremental phase tracking (frame-to-frame deltas instead of absolute phase) combined with ArUco optical flow fallback when marker detection drops out — reducing false positive rate significantly.
learnings: The most surprising finding was how inconsistent the UNCERTAIN band is. A frame-by-frame verdict flips between AI GENERATED and UNCERTAIN on the Kling output, which itself is a signal — authentic video produces stable scores, AI video produces unstable ones. The variance of the score distribution may be more diagnostic than the score itself.
futurePlans: Extend to shadow geometry (rigid object + known light source = fixed shadow angle), specular reflection (mirror must obey angle of incidence), and fluid dynamics (water ripple frequency set by surface tension + depth). Goal: a single passive prop kit that covers still camera, moving camera, and changing light — any one check failing raises a flag.

parts.label: Part 1 — The Totem (Still Camera)
parts.summary: A drinking glass placed in the scene acts as a refractive lens. Real video shows background refracted through the curved glass surface exactly as Snell's law predicts (n=1.5 glass, n=1.0 air). AI video generating pixels frame-by-frame cannot consistently reproduce this geometry — the refraction score drops and becomes erratic.
bullets: Detects the glass ellipse via Hough transform on each frame, fits the refractive boundary
Samples pixel pairs inside vs outside the glass boundary, computes Snell consistency score per frame
Authentic video: stable score ≥0.88 across frames (measured 0.91 and 0.94 on two real clips)
Kling AI output on same scene: score 0.862 (WARN) — drops toward the injection threshold of <0.70
Runs frame-by-frame with no pre-training — threshold values derived from the physics, not from data

parts.label: Part 2 — The Board (Moving Camera)
parts.summary: A printed fringe pattern with ArUco tracking markers placed alongside the glass. When the camera moves, the phase of the fringe pattern must shift in exact proportion to camera displacement — a hard geometric constraint. AI video hallucinates fringe movement uncorrelated with camera motion, causing phase variance to spike.
bullets: ArUco marker detection + optical flow fallback tracks marker positions on every frame
Warps the board region to original resolution using corner distances (no resize artifact) for accurate phase measurement
Tracks fringe phase incrementally (frame-to-frame deltas) to avoid periodic boundary jumps
Sliding-window Pearson correlation between camera displacement and phase shift classifies each window
Authentic video: phase std ≤0.04 rad; Kling AI output: 0.360 rad (9× over threshold) → FAIL

title: WayfinderAI
tagline: Won Hack@URI + Yconic · 100% graph connectivity, no GPS, no beacons
description: Two separate systems built toward the same goal: navigating indoor spaces without GPS, beacons, or custom hardware. Part 1 fine-tunes a vision-language model to read floor plans and output navigation graphs. Part 2 guides users through a real Kroger store using only the Kroger API, a phone camera, and local LLMs.

parts.label: Part 1 — VLM Floorplan Pipeline (NaviGrid)
parts.summary: Built a fully automated 3-phase pipeline to generate 4,248 VLM training pairs from 100 CubiCasa5K floor plans — zero manual annotation — then fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B via LoRA + GRPO to convert raw floor plan images into structured navigation graphs.
bullets: Phase 1: SVG parsing via ElementTree extracts room nodes (kitchen, hallway, bathroom, stairs) with bounding boxes and center coordinates

Phase 2: Algorithmic edge inference using proximity thresholds + corridor filtering + entrance-rooted BFS; direction-tagged ST/TL/TR/SA via atan2 geometry; LLaMA 3.2 generates plain English directions
Phase 3: 5-type QA pair generation (treemap, route, location-nav, spatial, multi-turn) → 4,248 pairs (3,824 train / 424 val) for Qwen3-VL fine-tuning
Baseline evaluation: direction similarity 0.746, plain English score 0.950, graph connectivity 100% — 8/15 inference successes (OOM crashes on remaining)
GRPO reward-based fine-tuning produced valid navigation graph JSON more reliably than supervised fine-tuning alone

media.caption: Navigation graph overlaid on floor plan — color-coded edges (Yellow=Straight, Blue=Left, Red=Right, Cyan=Side) and LLaMA-generated turn-by-turn instructions at the bottom

parts.label: Part 2 — Kroger Grocery Navigation App

media.caption: Full app walkthrough — natural language shopping input to aisle-by-aisle shelf directions
EasyOCR reads physical aisle signs every 5th frame to confirm real-world location
ArUco marker detection — optical flow fallback when OCR confidence drops

parts.summary: Five sequential functions guide users through a Kroger store — from natural language shopping input to real-time shelf-position guidance — using only the Kroger Developer API. No beacons, no GPS. Won 1st Place at Hack@URI AI Track (30+ teams).
bullets: Step 1: Kroger API → NetworkX graph (34 aisles, 110+ connections) built in <0.15s
Step 2: Ollama llama3.2 converts recipes or meal ideas → verified Kroger shopping list with live price checks
Step 3: Dual routing — Dijkstra in-order vs nearest-neighbor greedy; always picks 10–30% shorter path with real geometry-based turn directions
Step 4: EasyOCR reads physical aisle signs (A1–A42) every 5th frame to confirm real-world location; Claude Vision fallback on low-confidence reads
Step 5: YOLO-World open-vocabulary detection (no fine-tuning); 3-frame confirmation window; reports 9-region shelf position from bounding box centroid
FastAPI backend + React 18 frontend with interactive SVG store map and voice readout per direction

title: Apex AI
tagline: Won Twelve Labs + Cursor · cut lap times 0.75s from onboard video, no telemetry
description: AI race engineer that watches an onboard karting or motorcycle lap and delivers structured coaching — timestamped mistakes, best moments, sector scores, and lap time loss estimates. Built in two versions: one cloud-powered, one fully local.
inspiration: Most teams at the hackathon were executing familiar ideas and hoping implementation quality would win. I wanted to work on something I actually cared about — Formula 1. Race engineers extract insight from sensor telemetry; I wanted to do the same thing from video alone, with no hardware. That's where Apex AI came from.
challenges: V1: Twelve Labs returns rich but unstructured observations — getting Groq LLaMA to extract valid JSON performance scores without hallucinating required careful prompt engineering and retry logic. V2: Florence-2's object detection on CPU runs at 1–3s per frame. Running it on every frame would take hours, so I built a two-gate system: only triage keyframes flagged by the CV events loader, then only invoke llava on frames that pass Florence-2's severity threshold.
learnings: The API approach (V1) produces richer, more accurate coaching than anything a local pipeline can match today. But V2 showed that dividing the problem into small focused tasks — each handled by the right lightweight model — gets you surprisingly far without spending a dollar. The two versions aren't competing; they represent two different constraints, both worth understanding.

parts.label: V1 — PitLane AI (Twelve Labs)
parts.summary: Cloud-powered version using Twelve Labs Pegasus for whole-video semantic analysis and Marengo for timestamped video search. Won the Twelve Labs Computer Vision Hackathon at Northeastern University.
bullets: Pegasus watches the full lap and finds errors across 4 categories: Racing Line, Braking, Throttle & Traction, Car Control
Best Moments finder across 6 categories — smooth apex, clean acceleration, perfect racing line, and more
Free-form Q&A: 'Where am I losing the most time?' returns a verdict + timestamped moments
Coaching report: performance scores (1–10), sector breakdown, lap time loss in tenths of seconds, top 3 fixes
Two surfaces: FiftyOne plugin for dataset operators + React web app for live upload and review

parts.label: V2 — Apex AI (Fully Local)
parts.futurePlans: A more expert-driven approach would be stronger: purpose-built pipelines that only activate models relevant to the specific sport, delivering results shaped around what that discipline actually demands rather than a general coaching template.
parts.summary: Fully local 5-stage modular pipeline — no paid APIs, no internet required. Each stage is handled by a different lightweight model suited to that specific task. Supports karting, biking, and cycling from a single onboard video.
bullets: Stage 1: YOLOv8n + Farneback optical flow extracts braking, racing line, and speed delta events with severity scores
Stage 2: Florence-2-base (232M params, CPU) triages each keyframe — vehicle_visible, in_corner, obstacle_ahead via caption and object detection tasks
Stage 3: Conditional llava reasoning via Ollama — only fires on significant events or obstacle frames, skips the rest
Stage 4: Parallel llama3.2 coaching note writer — asyncio + ThreadPoolExecutor (4 workers) generates per-event notes concurrently
Stage 5: llama3.2 session aggregator synthesises all notes into a final structured coaching report
CV-only fallback mode when Ollama is unavailable — no hard dependency on a running LLM

title: Edge AI Multisensor System
tagline: 120× faster overheating response — 5 hub threads, local LLMs, no cloud
description: A two-level edge AI system for building HVAC management. Five parallel hub threads each monitor a dedicated zone using real BMS sensor data and three IAIF triggers to classify anomalies. A Central Validation Coordinator aggregates all hub reports and escalates cross-zone faults via Telegram — all AI runs locally via Ollama, no data leaves the building.
inspiration: Most commercial edge AI hubs already use LLMs — but only to present data. The actual fault detection still runs on hard thresholds written by engineers: if temp > X, flag it. I wanted to build something that could reason about whether a reading is actually anomalous in context, not just compare it to a number someone set during installation. The IAIF architecture gave me a framework for that — each hub maintains a belief state about its zone and updates it continuously, so the system detects divergence from expected behavior rather than just threshold violations.
challenges: The hardest problem was the CVC sync window: the coordinator needs to collect reports from all 5 hubs and aggregate them without blocking on a slow hub. The 12-second timeout had to be tight enough to catch real cross-zone anomalies but loose enough to tolerate hub latency spikes. The other challenge was separating moderate from critical at the hub level — moderate triggers hub-level LLM auto-correction, while critical events skip the hub LLM and go straight to CVC escalation.
learnings: The IAIF trigger structure is the key insight: the LLM only fires when Signal Lookout detects a genuine anomaly. In a clean building, Ollama never runs. This is the opposite of standard LLM pipelines where the model processes every data point — here the model is an exception handler, not a data processor. That constraint forces you to get the signal detection right before you ever think about the AI.

parts.label: Part 1 — Edge Hub Layer
parts.summary: Five independent hub threads each poll their zone every 5 seconds and run Signal Lookout — a 3-trigger IAIF gate that decides whether to invoke the LLM, auto-correct setpoints, or immediately escalate. Hub-1 monitors VAV-1–5 + RTU-6; Hub-2 monitors VAV-6–10 + RTU-9; Hub-3 monitors VAV-11–15 + RTU-10; Hub-4 monitors VAV-16–20 + RTU-11; Hub-5 monitors VAV-21–26.
bullets: Trigger 0 — Sensor Loss: new No Data zone detected (zone_temp goes None) → immediate critical, bypasses hub LLM, goes straight to CVC
Trigger 1 — Belief Divergence: divergence_score = (overheating + undercooled zones) / reportable zones; moderate >0.15, critical >0.40; RTU discharge <45°F also fires
Trigger 2 — EFE Power Error: actual PoE wattage >15% above expected (base 5000W + 50W × WiFi device count) → moderate
Moderate severity: hub Ollama llama3.2 fires, parses ADJUST commands, auto-corrects zone setpoints clamped ±5°F
Critical severity: hub skips local LLM entirely — report forwarded to CVC queue immediately for building-level reasoning
Inputs per cycle: VAV zone temps + setpoints, RTU discharge temps, Cisco WiFi device count, PoE switch wattage, Open-Meteo weather

parts.label: Part 2 — Central Validation Coordinator (CVC)
parts.summary: The CVC collects all 5 hub reports within a 12-second sync window, merges them into a building-level state, and runs a second Ollama llama3.2 pass if escalation criteria are met. Three action codes drive Telegram routing: URGENT/SHUTDOWN sends to both pipelines, MONITOR sends to the engineer only.
bullets: Escalates if: building severity = critical, cross-zone anomalies (≥2 hubs affected), ≥2 hub LLM failures, or building divergence score >0.40
Pipeline A → IoT Engineer: full diagnostic summary + action code (URGENT / MONITOR / SHUTDOWN)
Pipeline B → Building Operator: plain-language critical alert + inline Telegram buttons for acknowledge/override
9 named fault scenarios with exact sensor overrides: baseline, clean_slate, zone_overheat, too_cold, sensor_loss, power_surge, rtu_fault, multi_hub_crisis, full_storm, spike
Full JSONL event logging: hub_sensor_data, hub_prompt, hub_llm_response, hub_action, cvc_prompt, cvc_llm_response, cvc_action, ollama_failure, and more

title: Intelligent Follow-Me Robot
tagline: Tracks and reacquires a person through occlusion — YOLO + ReID + Kalman, zero GPU
description: A person-following robot that uses an Android phone as its only sensor — snapshot-polling video and streaming IMU data over WiFi to a Flask server running the full vision pipeline entirely on CPU. The server sends BLE motor commands to an Elegoo UNO R4 WiFi robot in real time.
longDescription: Each frame goes through YOLO26n detection, 3-zone MobileNetV2 ReID (head/upper/lower body embeddings + HSV histograms + gait), IoU-matched identity across frames, KCF tracking between YOLO frames, and Kalman smoothing. A visual odometry module tracks heading and yaw drift per frame. Every command requires 2-frame confirmation before firing. A 3-stage safety pipeline gates all output. When the target is lost, gyro-integrated search sweeps drive re-acquisition.
highlights: Android phone as the only sensor — IP Webcam /shot.jpg snapshot polling + DeviceMotion IMU at ~50Hz
3-zone ReID: MobileNetV2 embeddings (head/upper/lower body) + HSV histograms + gait; IoU matching (≥0.20) between frames prevents stale identity bugs
Visual odometry: heading_deg and delta_yaw tracked per frame via optical flow to inform directional control
Command debouncing: 2-frame confirmation before any BLE command fires; person-fleeing bypass when area_ratio < 0.15
Hard YOLO veto: zero-person detection immediately overrides tracker output, preventing wall-drift
3-stage safety pipeline: Step 32 obstacle heuristics → local reflex layer → safety governor
challenges: The KCF tracker drifts onto walls when the target is lost — fixed with a hard YOLO veto: if YOLO runs and finds zero people, tracker output is discarded entirely. ReID suffered a stale index bug when person detections shifted between frames — solved by IoU-matching the current bounding box against the previous frame before committing to a gallery update (threshold ≥ 0.20).
learnings: The IMU isn't tracking the person — it's tracking the robot. Using accelerometer shake to skip ReID on blurry frames and gyro yaw to gate tracker re-init during fast turns made the system dramatically more robust without adding any extra sensors. The 2-frame command confirmation eliminated jitter from spurious BLE commands, while the fleeing-person bypass preserved instant response when the target moved away fast.

title: Star Tracker CNN
tagline: 91% detection accuracy, 3.86× INT8 compression — ELUNet star tracker for Raspberry Pi
description: Research project benchmarking three U-Net architectures for star detection and sub-pixel centroid localisation on real DSS2 sky images, under strict CubeSat constraints: model size, inference speed, and accuracy all matter equally.
longDescription: Trained and evaluated UNet (482K params), MobileUNet (255K params), and ELUNet (60K params) on 250 real 256×256 sky images from NASA SkyView's DSS2 Red Survey. ELUNet uses a dual-channel output head — segmentation + distance map regression — enabling trilateration-based sub-pixel centroiding. INT8 quantization compresses ELUNet from 232 KB to 60 KB with less than 0.003 F1 loss, making it the strongest candidate for Raspberry Pi deployment.
highlights: Three architectures compared: UNet (482K params), MobileUNet (255K), ELUNet (60K — based on arXiv:2404.19108)
Ground truth segmentation maps generated by Gaussian blur → brightness thresholding → connected component size filtering on 250 real DSS2 sky images
ELUNet dual-channel head: segmentation + distance map regression → trilateration-based sub-pixel centroiding, no post-processing required
INT8 quantization via LSQ (Learned Step Size) fine-tuning: 232 KB → 60 KB (3.86× compression), F1 drop < 0.003
Part of the Northeastern Satellite Lab CubeSat Star Tracker project — targeting Raspberry Pi deployment under strict power and size constraints
challenges: MobileUNet — despite having fewer parameters than UNet — was the slowest at inference. The inverted residual blocks with depthwise separable convolutions that make MobileNet efficient on classification don't translate well to dense segmentation at 256×256 resolution. ELUNet's single-conv blocks with batch norm proved both faster and more quantization-friendly.
learnings: The metric that matters for satellite hardware isn't F1 alone — it's F1 per millisecond per kilobyte. ELUNet's aggressive channel reduction (base_ch=8 vs 16 for UNet) and single-conv blocks make it quantization-friendly: INT8 drops F1 by only 0.003 while cutting size 3.86×. The dual output head gave sub-pixel centroid accuracy through trilateration without adding any post-processing overhead.
